questions.text: Walk me through what happens when you type a URL and press Enter.
questions.answer: URL parse → caches/HSTS → DNS → routing → TCP or QUIC → TLS → HTTP request → edge/LB → proxy → app → DB → response → parse/render → subresources. Name a measurement tool for each stage. End by offering to go deeper on one layer.

questions.text: Which of these stages can only be measured client-side, and why does that matter?
questions.answer: Rendering, subresource waterfall, and the true DNS/TCP/TLS timing as experienced by the user. The server can't see client queueing or parse time. Implication: correlate RUM with server logs via a request ID, or you'll optimise the wrong thing.

questions.text: How do you attribute 800 ms of TTFB?
questions.answer: curl -w for the client-side split, then nginx $request_time vs $upstream_response_time to separate edge from app, then APM/DB slow-query data for the app split. A - in urt means the request never reached upstream.

questions.text: Why does HTTP/2 remove head-of-line blocking but not eliminate it?
questions.answer: It removes *application-level* HOL (streams are independent), but all streams share one ordered TCP byte stream, so a lost packet still delays everything. QUIC fixes that with independent per-stream loss recovery.

questions.text: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: the one-sentence version.
questions.answer: 1.1 is one request at a time per connection with many connections; 2 is many streams on one connection with HPACK; 3 is many streams on one connection over QUIC with no transport HOL and 0/1-RTT handshakes.

questions.text: Explain TCP's three-way handshake and why it needs three packets.
questions.answer: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Two would leave the server unable to confirm the client can receive, allowing blind spoofing, and options (MSS, SACK, timestamps, window scale) need exchanging. Costs a full RTT.

questions.text: What's the difference between flow control and congestion control?
questions.answer: Flow control protects the receiver (window based on free buffer, zero-window probes). Congestion control protects the network (slow start, AIMD, fast recovery, BBR). Confusing them is a classic interview tell.

questions.text: Explain Nagle's algorithm and the delayed-ACK 40 ms interaction.
questions.answer: Nagle holds a small unacknowledged write; the peer's delayed ACK waits up to 40 ms. Result: ~40 ms latency on small interactive writes. Fixes: TCP_NODELAY, TCP_QUICKACK, batching writes, or a framing protocol that isn't byte-stream-shaped.

questions.text: What is TIME_WAIT for, and what happens when you have too many?
questions.answer: It lingers for 2×MSL so delayed duplicates can't be mistaken for a new connection on the same 4-tuple. Too many exhaust ephemeral ports (EADDRNOTAVAIL). Fix: reuse connections, tcp_tw_reuse, wider port range, and above all stop churning connections.

questions.text: Why is tcp_tw_recycle dangerous and deprecated?
questions.answer: It disabled the TCP timestamp option toward a peer after a TIME_WAIT burst, which breaks connections from clients behind NAT/CGNAT because timestamps appear to go backwards. Removed in Linux 4.12. Use tcp_tw_reuse and reduce churn.

questions.text: What is a SYN cookie and when does it help?
questions.answer: When the SYN queue is full, the kernel encodes the connection state into the ISN instead of allocating memory, so legitimate SYNs still succeed. It helps against SYN floods.

questions.text: What does SO_REUSEPORT do and what's the trade-off?
questions.answer: Multiple sockets can bind the same address:port, and the kernel distributes incoming connections among them — that's how Nginx/Node scale workers. Trade-off: distribution is per-flow and can't be weighted, and rebinding with different configs is error-prone.

questions.text: When would you choose UDP for a new service?
questions.answer: Real-time media (latency beats loss), QUIC, DNS/NTP/telemetry, and custom-protocol cases. The obligation: you must implement your own congestion control, or you'll be a bad network citizen and get rate-limited.

ClientHello (version, ciphers, SNI, ALPN, key_share) → ServerHello + EE + Certificate + CertificateVerify + Finished → client validates chain/hostname/date → client Finished. 1-RTT because data follows the client's Finished.

questions.text: What does forward secrecy mean, and which key exchange gives it?
questions.answer: Recorded traffic can't be decrypted if the long-term key is later stolen. Ephemeral (EC)DHE gives it; static RSA does not. TLS 1.3 removed static RSA entirely.

questions.text: Why is SNI plaintext a privacy problem, and what fixes it?
questions.answer: The ClientHello is unencrypted, so the hostname is visible to any on-path observer. ECH (Encrypted ClientHello) encrypts the inner ClientHello under a public key from a DNS HTTPS record.

questions.text: What exactly does the client check in certificate validation?
questions.answer: Chain to a trusted root, each signature, validity dates, hostname against SAN (not CN), key usage and extended key usage, basic constraints, and (if configured) revocation.
No. Browsers soft-fail and often skip it; CRLs are stale; Let's Encrypt has no OCSP. The modern answer is short-lived certificates with automated renewal, with stapling as an improvement.

questions.text: TLS termination at the edge or in the app?
questions.answer: Edge: one cert, one cipher policy, HTTP/2/3 at the edge, easy WAF — but the plaintext leg must be trusted. App: real client IP, no double handshake, but N certs to manage. Re-encrypting between the two is common in regulated setups.
Without SNI a shared IP returns the default certificate, so you'd diagnose the wrong cert. Always pass -servername when the host is virtual-hosted.

questions.text: GET vs POST vs PUT vs PATCH vs DELETE: safety and idempotency.
questions.answer: Safe = no state change (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/TRACE). Idempotent = same effect if repeated (GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE, and PATCH only with idempotent patch semantics). POST is neither. Proxies may retry idempotent methods, so use an Idempotency-Key for POST creates.
401 = not authenticated (needs WWW-Authenticate); 403 = authenticated but not allowed; 404 = no such resource (sometimes used deliberately to hide 403s, at the cost of API clarity).

502 = upstream connection failed or response invalid; 503 = no healthy upstreams or shedding; 504 = upstream too slow; 499 (nginx) = client gave up. 502 vs 504 is the most useful distinction: broken vs slow.
301 permanent (cacheable, may rewrite method), 302 temporary (historical GET rewrite), 307/308 preserve method and body (temporary/permanent). 303 is the post/redirect/get.

questions.text: What does Cache-Control: no-cache actually do?
questions.answer: It does not mean "don't store". It means "store it, but revalidate before every use". no-store means never store. max-age=0 is similar to no-cache in effect.

questions.text: Explain the Vary header and a real bug it prevents.
questions.answer: It tells caches which request headers changed the representation. Without Vary: Accept-Encoding, a CDN serves a brotli body to a gzip-only client; without Vary: Origin, a CORS response for one origin is served to another.

questions.text: What are Transfer-Encoding: chunked and why is it banned in HTTP/2?
questions.answer: It provides framing for an HTTP/1.1 response of unknown length. HTTP/2 has native frame and stream length, so the header is forbidden; allowing it enabled request-smuggling and response-splitting attacks.
Letting the server reject an oversized or unauthorised upload by Content-Length before the client sends the body. Real bandwidth and DoS savings. Answer 417/403 to refuse.

questions.text: Explain ETag vs Last-Modified, and If-Range.
questions.answer: ETags are opaque validators (strong "x", weak W/"x") and are more reliable than a 1-second-resolution date. If-Range lets a resumed download verify the entity didn't change; if it did, the server returns the full body and the client starts over.

questions.text: When is compression worth it, and what is BREACH?
questions.answer: Compress text (HTML/CSS/JS/JSON/SVG), skip already-compressed types, threshold around 1 KB, and always Vary: Accept-Encoding. BREACH: mixing secrets with attacker-controlled input in a compressed TLS response lets an attacker extract the secret from the compressed size — don't reflect input into compressed authenticated pages.
Responses must be read in order, so a slow first response blocks everything behind it — the same HOL problem — and intermediaries implemented it inconsistently. HTTP/2's multiplexing replaced it.

questions.text: Explain HPACK and where header leaks come from.
questions.answer: Static table + dynamic table + Huffman. If a decoder mixes up table state across connections or requests, values from one response can appear in another. Implementation correctness is a security boundary.

First GOAWAY with last-stream-id = 2^31−1 and no error code = "stop creating new streams"; second with the real last-stream-id = the final boundary. Sending only the first and then dropping connections causes 502 storms.

questions.text: Explain per-stream vs connection-level flow control in HTTP/2.
questions.answer: Each stream has its own window and each sends WINDOW_UPDATE; there's also a connection-level window. If the connection window hits zero, all streams stall. Changing INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE doesn't affect existing streams; each needs an explicit WINDOW_UPDATE.

questions.text: What is QPACK and how is it better than HPACK?
questions.answer: QPACK (HTTP/3) has a static table, a dynamic table, and — key difference — dynamic-table insertions happen on a separate encoder stream, so header compression is no longer blocked on a round trip.

questions.text: Why is 0-RTT replayable, and what do you do about it?
questions.answer: The server can't distinguish a genuine early-data request from a replay of captured Initial packets. So: only idempotent operations, disable 0-RTT on mutating endpoints, or require a token bound to the request.

questions.text: What does Alt-Svc do and what's the risk of a long ma?
questions.answer: It advertises an alternative (usually HTTP/3) endpoint. The client tries it and pins for the ma window. A long ma means a transient UDP block can cost you HTTP/3 for that user for weeks. Roll out with a short ma first.

questions.text: CDN: what is the cache key, and why do tracking params hurt?
questions.answer: Typically scheme+host+path+query plus configured headers. ?utm_* params multiply the key space so almost everything misses. Strip known tracking params at the edge or normalise.

questions.text: What is shielding, and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: A parent/shield tier that regional edges pull from, so a cache miss doesn't send every POP to the origin simultaneously. Prevents a thundering herd on a burst of new or invalidated content.

questions.text: When is a CDN a DDoS control, and when isn't it?
questions.answer: Good at volumetric L3/L4 floods and generic L7 floods (anycast + WAF + rate limiting). Not at business-logic abuse, expensive non-cacheable endpoints, or when the origin is reachable directly. The origin must accept only the CDN's ranges.

Any client can prepend a fake entry. Each honest proxy appends. So the right-most entry from a proxy you control is the closest thing to a real client IP. Better: edge overwrites X-Real-IP, or use the PROXY protocol.

L4 decides on IP/port, sees no body, is fastest and protocol-agnostic (works for QUIC). L7 sees the request, so it can route by path, cache, compress, WAF, and see the real client IP — at a CPU and latency cost.

questions.text: Compare round robin, least connections, IP hash, and consistent hashing.
questions.answer: RR is simple and breaks with uneven request cost. Least connections suits long-lived connections but ignores duration. IP hash gives affinity but remaps on scale and collapses behind CGNAT. Consistent hashing minimises remapping and is right for large local caches.

questions.text: Active vs passive health checks, slow start, hysteresis.
questions.answer: Active detects a hung-but-listening server; passive only learns from real errors. Slow start ramps traffic so a cold instance isn't hammered. Hysteresis (N successes / M failures) prevents flapping from a single dropped probe.

questions.text: When is a sticky session the right answer?
questions.answer: When state is in process memory. Better: externalise state so you don't need it. If you must, use a signed cookie or a token-derived key rather than IP hashing.

questions.text: Explain graceful shutdown behind a load balancer.
questions.answer: Mark the target draining, stop new traffic, send Connection: close/GOAWAY on in-flight responses, have the app finish work on SIGTERM, then remove it once connections drain or a deadline passes. Without it you get a 502 storm on every deploy.

questions.text: Read this nginx log: rt=1.842 uct=0.002 urt=1.838.
questions.answer: The app took 1.838 s; connecting to it took 2 ms. Network and connections are fine. Attack application and database time.

questions.text: Read this: rt=0.001 urt=- with a 503.
questions.answer: The request never reached upstream. A load balancer with no healthy targets, a rate-limit rejection, or a size/header check. Correlate by request ID with origin logs.

questions.text: WebSocket handshake: what is Sec-WebSocket-Accept for?
questions.answer: base64(SHA1(key + GUID)). It's a protocol marker proving the server speaks WebSockets and defeating proxy caching of the upgrade — it is not authentication.

questions.text: Why must WebSocket clients mask frames?
questions.answer: To stop cache poisoning: a client can always produce different bytes for the same logical request, so a proxy can't confuse a request with a cached response. It's a spec security requirement, not an optimisation.

questions.text: Close code 1006: what does it mean?
questions.answer: The connection closed with no close frame — a timeout, a reset, or a network drop. Servers can't send it. If the duration is a round number, suspect an intermediary idle timeout; fix with heartbeats below the shortest timeout in the chain.

questions.text: gRPC: why is every call HTTP 200, and what does it break?
questions.answer: Status is in grpc-status in the trailers, not the HTTP status. So HTTP-level metrics, LB health checks, and retry middleware all see success. Monitor gRPC status and disable automatic retries for non-idempotent methods.

questions.text: How do gRPC deadlines propagate, and what if they're wrong?
questions.answer: The client sets grpc-timeout; the server enforces it and cancels, returning DEADLINE_EXCEEDED with RetryInfo. A client deadline longer than its upstream's means the upstream gives up first — set them deliberately, tighter as you go down.

questions.text: Five honest reasons not to use gRPC for a public API.
questions.answer: No HTTP caching (POST + body), hard to debug without grpcurl, Protobuf isn't human-readable, browsers need gRPC-Web and lose client/bidi streaming, and proxies/gateways handle it poorly.

questions.text: GraphQL over HTTP: why is the response usually 200 with errors?
questions.answer: The spec puts errors in the body, and implementations mostly keep the HTTP status at 200. So HTTP monitoring sees success. Instrument per-operation, not per-request.

questions.text: Why is a GraphQL query harder to cache than a REST resource?
questions.answer: The response depends on the entire document, not a URL. A CDN can only cache it if every field resolution respects Cache-Control and Vary, which is impractical.

questions.text: What are depth and complexity limits for, and what does depth miss?
questions.answer: Depth caps nesting; complexity analysis multiplies each field by its list-size multiplier (first: 10000); total-field caps catch wide-but-shallow queries. Aliases let one query request an expensive field many times — depth alone misses all of this.

questions.text: CORS: what exactly does the browser check?
questions.answer: Origin matches Access-Control-Allow-Origin (exact, or * only when not credentialed); for preflight, the method is in Allow-Methods and the headers in Allow-Headers; with credentials, exact origin plus Allow-Credentials: true.

questions.text: Why is CORS not a CSRF defence?
questions.answer: It gates whether page script can *read* a response, not whether a request is *sent*. A form POST with a safelisted content type is sent cross-site with the victim's cookies and no preflight. Use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.

questions.text: Why is Allow-Origin: * invalid with credentials, and why does Allow-Headers: * also fail there?
questions.answer: The wildcard means "any origin, but not with credentials" and the spec forbids combining it with Allow-Credentials: true. And Allow-Headers: * is treated as a literal header name for credentialed requests, not a wildcard.

questions.text: Why must CORS responses have Vary: Origin?
questions.answer: Because the response differs by Origin; without Vary, a shared cache can serve one origin's response to another, which the browser then rejects — or leaks allowlist information.
Auth middleware is running on OPTIONS. The browser sends the preflight without credentials, so you must skip auth (or return 204) for OPTIONS.

questions.text: How do you debug a CORS failure systematically?
questions.answer: Read the console message (it names the check), find the OPTIONS request in the Network tab and its status, reproduce with curl -X OPTIONS including Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method, compare the returned origin to the request origin exactly, check credentials mode, check for a redirect, and re-test with caching disabled.

questions.text: SMTPS: ports 25, 587, 465, and why must you never send from 25?
questions.answer: 25 is server-to-server relay (no auth, often blocked, and an open relay gets you blocklisted); 587 is authenticated submission (use this); 465 is implicit-TLS submission.

questions.text: What do SPF, DKIM, and DMARC each assert, and what is alignment?
questions.answer: SPF: which hosts may send as this envelope domain. DKIM: the body and headers are unaltered and signed by a holder of the domain's key. DMARC: what to do when SPF *or* DKIM fails, plus reporting. Alignment = the visible From domain matches the SPF envelope domain or the DKIM d= domain.

questions.text: Why does forwarded email usually pass DMARC even though SPF fails?
questions.answer: Forwarding breaks SPF (the forwarder isn't authorised), but the From header and DKIM signature are preserved, so DKIM stays aligned with From. DMARC passes on DKIM.

5.x.x is permanent (no such mailbox, policy rejection) — never retry, suppress the address. 4.x.x is transient (busy, quota, greylisted) — retry with exponential backoff. Re-sending to hard bounces is a reputation and often legal problem.

questions.text: STUN vs TURN, and when is TURN unavoidable?
questions.answer: STUN discovers your public address (server-reflexive candidate). TURN relays media when a direct path is impossible (symmetric NAT, restrictive corporate firewalls). TURN costs money and adds latency, and a high relay rate means your edge is the bottleneck.

questions.text: What is SDP and why is it an offer/answer exchange?
questions.answer: SDP describes codecs, fingerprints, and candidates. One side offers capabilities, the other answers with what it can accept, because both must agree before media can flow. You exchange it over your own signalling channel.

questions.text: How do you measure WebRTC call quality?
questions.answer: From getStats(): the selected ICE candidate pair (host/server-reflexive/TURN), packets lost, jitter, RTT, current bitrate and frame size, jitter-buffer delay. A TURN-selected pair points to network, not application.

questions.text: Explain an MTU black hole and how to find it.
questions.answer: A smaller path MTU with ICMP PTB messages filtered, so large packets vanish silently while small ones and DNS work. Find it with ping -M do -s <size> (binary-search the size, add 28 for the header) and tracepath. Fix the tunnel MTU, clamp MSS, and never blanket-block ICMP.

questions.text: Explain bufferbloat and how it hurts a web app.
questions.answer: Oversized router buffers create long queues; latency balloons under load even though throughput is fine. Fix with AQM/fq/cake on the router. For a server, it's the analogue of an oversized connection pool.

questions.text: What does Age in a cache response tell you?
questions.answer: How long the object has been cached. Large Age on a deploy means a stale object is being served; combined with X-Cache: HIT it's the direct evidence you need for a stale-content investigation.

questions.text: Your API returns 429 without CORS headers, and the browser reports a CORS error. Explain.
questions.answer: The browser only surfaces CORS failures to script, so it masks the real status. A 429 from a rate limiter that doesn't include CORS headers looks like a CORS problem. Fix: put CORS on all error paths, and fix the rate limiter's key (behind a CDN, X-Forwarded-For may be the CDN's IP for everyone).

questions.text: What are the DNS cache layers?
questions.answer: Browser, OS/systemd-resolved, recursive resolver, and the authoritative server's own view
lookup uses the OS resolver (hosts, NSS, search domains) and the libuv thread pool; resolve4 talks DNS directly over the wire

questions.text: Why can't a CNAME have an MX record?
questions.answer: A CNAME must be the only record at that name; use a separate host for mail, or an ALIAS/ANAME
min(SOA.MINIMUM, SOA.TTL) per RFC 2308; surprises deployers for minutes after a bad record

questions.text: Lowering a TTL: why doesn't it take effect immediately?
questions.answer: Existing cache entries keep their original expiry; convergence is bounded by the old TTL plus browser/OS caches
Vendor-specific apex alias, since a CNAME is illegal at the apex (SOA and NS live there)

questions.text: What does a CNAME at the apex break?
questions.answer: Zone apex must carry SOA and NS; RFC 1034 §3.6.2 forbids a CNAME there
Same name, different answers inside vs outside; the classic "works at home, not in the office" cause

questions.text: What does DNSSEC protect and not protect?
questions.answer: Authenticity and integrity of records; not confidentiality, and revocation is separate

questions.text: How does a bad DS record manifest?
questions.answer: SERVFAIL for validating resolvers while non-validating ones still resolve
20 bytes (+options) vs 8; that's where all the difference in ceremony starts

questions.text: Why is TCP a byte stream and UDP a datagram?
questions.answer: TCP sequences bytes with no message boundaries; UDP preserves them. Bugs follow: reads must buffer and parse

questions.text: TCP three-way handshake: what do the options carry?
questions.answer: MSS, SACK-permitted, timestamps, window scale — all negotiated in the first flight
Receiver's buffer vs the network; windows vs slow start/AIMD
Exponential cwnd doubling to ssthresh, then linear congestion avoidance; 3 duplicate ACKs → fast recovery
A specific loss, not congestion; trigger fast retransmit/recovery instead of a slow-start restart
Never take an RTT sample from a retransmitted segment; you can't tell which copy was delayed
TCP (one ordered stream), HTTP/1.1 (in-order responses); HTTP/2 fixes only the HTTP layer; QUIC fixes transport
Up to 40 ms on small writes; fix with TCP_NODELAY or batching
Sender pings a receiver whose buffer is full so it can reopen the window and avoid deadlock
2×MSL so late duplicates can't be confused with a new connection on the same 4-tuple
Usually the client (it initiates the close); 40k sockets = ephemeral port exhaustion
Multiple listeners on one port, kernel distributes flows; how Nginx/Node scale workers
Encode state in the ISN when the SYN queue is full; defeats SYN floods
MSS = MTU − 40 (IPv4 TCP header) − 20 (TCP header) = MTU − 60
DNS and small requests work, TLS/large requests hang; find it with ping -M do -s and tracepath
Confidentiality, integrity, server authentication (and client auth with mTLS)
1-RTT (0-RTT on resumption); the client's data follows its Finished
Static RSA, CBC ciphers, compression, renegotiation, most negotiation round trips
Encryption + auth tag in one operation; removed the CBC padding-oracle family of bugs
Ephemeral (EC)DHE; a stolen long-term key doesn't reveal recorded traffic. TLS 1.3 has it by default

questions.text: What is SNI and why is it a problem?
questions.answer: The hostname in a plaintext ClientHello; needed for shared-IP hosting, but it leaks what you visit. ECH fixes it
Negotiating h2/h3 vs http/1.1 on one port; how HTTP/2 avoids the Upgrade dance
0-RTT (replayable) and 1-RTT (safe); session tickets are self-contained and need key rotation
The server can't distinguish real early data from a replay; only idempotent operations

questions.text: OCSP vs stapling vs revocation reality?
questions.answer: OCSP is an online query; stapling pre-fetches it; in practice browsers soft-fail and LE has no OCSP, so short-lived certs win
Cert demands a stapled status; clients refuse otherwise; the real fix for soft-fail, limited deployment
A client cert proves identity; it says nothing about permissions — keep the app-level check
Yes, or you get the default cert on a shared IP and diagnose the wrong thing

questions.text: How do you read a cipher suite name?
questions.answer: Kx-Au-Enc-Mac, e.g. ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 = ephemeral EC key exchange, RSA cert, AES-GCM, SHA-256
Safe = no state change; idempotent = repeatable with the same effect. DELETE is idempotent but not safe
Not authenticated (needs WWW-Authenticate) vs authenticated but not allowed
Upstream connection failed/invalid response vs upstream too slow
nginx's "client closed request" — a latency signal, not a server-health one
Both permanent; 308 preserves method and body, 301 historically invites method rewriting
307 preserves method and body; 302 is temporary and may become GET
Revalidate before use vs never store at all
Telling caches which request headers changed the representation; get it wrong and you serve the wrong variant
"abc" byte-exact vs W/"abc" semantically equal; use strong for byte ranges
HTTP/1.1 framing for unknown length; forbidden in HTTP/2, which is why it was a smuggling vector

questions.text: Which headers are banned in HTTP/2?
questions.answer: Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Connection, TE (except trailers), Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade
:method, :scheme, :authority, :path — lowercase, before regular headers; CONNECT omits scheme/path
DATA, HEADERS, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, GOAWAY, PING, PRIORITY, PUSH_PROMISE, CONTINUATION
Same idea; QPACK's dynamic table updates ride a separate encoder stream, so they don't block on a round trip

questions.text: Is server push still a thing?
questions.answer: Removed from all major browsers; use preload, 103 Early Hints, and speculative connections
A zero connection-level window stalls every stream; changing INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE doesn't fix existing streams
One TLS connection shared across hostnames the cert covers; good for latency, confusing for capacity planning

questions.text: Why can HTTP/2 still be slow?
questions.answer: TCP head-of-line blocking, small writes + Nagle, stream limits, and a server that lost its connection-level parallelism
1-RTT/0-RTT handshakes, no transport HOL, per-stream loss recovery, connection migration
Packet payload AEAD plus header protection (first byte and packet number)
Connection ID, not a 4-tuple, which is what enables migration across networks
Server advertises, client tries and pins for ma; start with a short ma, never advertise without a real h3 listener
Forward sits in front of clients (egress, anonymity); reverse sits in front of servers (TLS, LB, cache, WAF)
L4 sees IP/port only (fast, protocol-agnostic, needs QUIC-aware LBs); L7 sees the request (routing, caching, real client IP)
Ignores request cost and connection duration; a slow backend still gets equal share
Counts connections, not work; a slow long request still counts as one
Remaps everything on scale, collapses behind CGNAT, ignores load
Large local caches; only affected keys move when a backend leaves
Active catches a hung-but-listening server; passive only learns from real user errors
Ramp traffic to a new target; require N passes / M failures so one dropped probe doesn't evict a good server
A DB blip then fails every instance at once and removes all capacity
Right-most entry from a proxy you control; the left-most is attacker-controlled
A layer-4 header the LB sets and the edge strips; can't be forged by an external client
Pull fetches from origin on a miss (default); push pre-warms the edge for a launch or a livestream
Scheme + host + path + query (+ configured headers); tracking params multiply the key space and kill the hit rate
A parent tier so regional edges don't all hit origin on a miss; prevents a stampede
Serve stale immediately, refresh in the background; trades freshness for latency
HMAC over the path plus an expiry, validated at the edge; private content through a shared cache

questions.text: When is a CDN not DDoS protection?
questions.answer: Business-logic abuse, expensive non-cacheable paths, and any attack that can reach the origin directly
Clears the hop-by-hop header so upstream keep-alive works; needs proxy_http_version 1.1
SPA fallback: serve the file if it exists, else the shell, so deep links work
Reading = slow clients sending; Writing = clients not reading the response
base64(SHA1(key + GUID)); a protocol marker, not authentication
FIN, RSV1-3, opcode, MASK, 7-bit length (+16/64-bit extension), 4-byte mask, payload
Cache poisoning: a masked request can't be mistaken for a cached response. A spec security requirement
0 continuation, 1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pong
Abnormal closure, no close frame exchanged; a timeout, reset, or network drop. Servers can't send it
Going away — the right code on a deploy so clients reconnect to a new instance
No: small CPU/memory cost, marginal gain, and most stacks disable it. Use no_context_takeover if you do
Forward Upgrade and Connection, use proxy_http_version 1.1, long read timeout, proxy_buffering off, heartbeats below the shortest idle timeout
Bound the per-connection send queue; drop the oldest or close the client. Unbounded queues are an OOM during a slow-client incident
te: trailers, Content-Type: application/grpc+proto, and status in trailers — that's why it's required

questions.text: Why is every gRPC call a POST?
questions.answer: The method is in the path (/package.Service/Method); HTTP method carries no semantics
1 byte compression flag + 4-byte big-endian length + the Protobuf bytes
UNAVAILABLE, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (with RetryInfo), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED for idempotent calls, ABORTED at a higher level. Never INVALID_ARGUMENT or PERMISSION_DENIED
Without jitter every client reconnects at the same instant after a deploy — a self-inflicted stampede
One HTTP/2 connection carries many calls, so naive round-robin at the channel level fails; use round_robin/grpclb/xDS or a mesh
A complete map of your internal API surface; disable it or gate it behind auth
Unary and server streaming only; no client or bidi streaming in browsers, because fetch can't send a streaming request body
POST with {"query", "variables", "operationName"}; GET allowed for queries only (cacheable); response is usually 200 even with errors
An array of operations in one request; saves round trips but multiplies rate-limit and cost exposure, so the spec deprecated it
Client sends a hash; server says not found, client sends the full text once; then hash-only. Bandwidth saving plus an effective allowlist
Depth caps nesting; complexity multiplies fields by list-size multipliers; field count catches wide alias abuse. Depth alone misses all of it
graphql-transport-ws over WebSockets with typed messages and per-subscription IDs; subscriptions-transport-ws is deprecated
SSE: auto-reconnect, Last-Event-ID resumption, proxy-friendly, but no client→server channel
Codecs, fingerprints, and ICE candidates, in an offer/answer exchange over your own signalling
STUN finds your public address; TURN relays when a direct path is impossible (symmetric NAT, corporate firewalls)

questions.text: Why is media end-to-end encrypted by default?
questions.answer: DTLS-SRTP negotiated via the SDP fingerprints. An SFU terminates the media, which breaks naive E2E claims
Send candidates as they're found instead of waiting, so connection starts sooner; needs a live signalling channel
P2P reliable-ordered or unreliable-unordered channel over the same connection; good for ephemeral low-latency data
25 relay (no auth, often blocked, never for apps), 587 authenticated submission, 465 implicit-TLS submission
A server that relays for anyone; discovered within hours, then blocklisted everywhere. Never expose one
Lower wins; equal values mean the sender tries them in arbitrary order. A null MX (0 .) says "no mail here"
The 10-lookup limit with include: chains, and forwarding (the forwarder's IP isn't authorised)
A canonicalised set of headers plus the body; the key is in DNS at selector._domainkey
A policy for SPF/DKIM failure, reporting via rua=, and alignment between the visible From and SPF/DKIM

questions.text: Why do forwarded emails pass DMARC?
questions.answer: SPF fails but DKIM stays aligned with the preserved From, and DMARC passes on DKIM
5.x.x permanent: suppress, never retry. 4.x.x transient: back off and retry
IMAP is server-side state (folders, flags, sync, partial fetch); POP3 is download-and-delete. Apps send over SMTP and never need IMAP
Scheme + host + port must all match; the port is the part people forget
GET/HEAD/POST with a safelisted Content-Type (form-urlencoded, multipart, text/plain) and only safelisted headers
Not a safelisted content type, so the browser sends OPTIONS first

questions.text: What must a preflight response include?
questions.answer: Allow-Origin matching, Allow-Methods with the method, Allow-Headers with any non-safelisted headers, and optionally Max-Age

questions.text: Why is CORS not a CSRF control?
questions.answer: It gates reading, not sending. A form POST with a safelisted type reaches your server with the victim's cookies and no preflight
Nothing changes on the server; curl and mobile apps ignore it entirely. It's a browser read policy, not authentication
Invalid; the browser rejects it. Credentialed requests need an exact origin plus Allow-Credentials: true
Treated as the literal header name *, so it doesn't work; list the headers explicitly
Mandatory on CORS responses, or a shared cache serves one origin's response to another
Auth middleware is running on OPTIONS; skip auth and return 204 with the CORS headers
Middleware mounted after routes, so errors and even 200s from early handlers lack the headers
Reject an oversized or unauthorised upload from Content-Length before the client sends the body
Resume only if the validator still matches; if not, return the full 200 so the client starts over safely
br best ratio for static, gzip universal, zstd fastest with good ratio; skip already-compressed types
Compressing a response that mixes secrets with attacker-controlled input lets the attacker recover the secret from the compressed size

questions.text: Long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket?
questions.answer: Long polling: trivial and proxy-hostile to connections; SSE: one-way with auto-reconnect; WebSocket: full duplex
Host required, persistent by default, chunked encoding, real caching and range support
Explicit length enables progress and keep-alive framing; chunked streams unknown lengths (HTTP/1.1 only)
Seconds or a date on 429 and 503, so clients back off instead of hammering
RFC 7239 is structured (for=, proto=, host=); the X- headers are the de facto convention. Both need a proxy trust list
HSTS: force HTTPS for max-age, optionally with includeSubDomains/preload; only honoured over HTTPS

TCP and UDP

[ ] I can separate flow control from congestion control and name the failure each prevents
[ ] I know slow start, ssthresh, congestion avoidance, fast recovery, SRTT/RTTVAR, and Karn's algorithm
[ ] I can explain head-of-line blocking at the TCP, HTTP/1.1, and HTTP/2 layers

TLS

practice.markdown:
Model answers are written to be spoken: they lead with the decision, give the reason, name

practice.title: -7.21 RAPID-FIRE
practice.afterTopic: Secure defaults, fail-closed, and fail-open trade-offs
items: 7.17 Authentication
Cookie or localStorage for a bearer token? HttpOnly cookie — XSS is hard to prevent, CSRF is easy; the cookie makes the harder problem not catastrophic.
Why not encrypt the JWT instead? An access token's claims are not secret from its holder, so JWE adds key-distribution cost and no security.
Name the four cookie attributes that matter. HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, and host-only (no Domain).
Best SameSite value for a session cookie? Lax — kills classic CSRF without breaking inbound links.
What does SameSite=Lax still allow? A top-level cross-site GET navigation, so never mutate state on GET.
What is a cookie prefix and why use it? __Host- requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain, so the browser rejects a subdomain trying to set or shadow it.
Minimum entropy for a session ID? 128 bits from a CSPRNG; I use 256.
Never use Math.random() for? Session IDs, tokens, salts, nonces, CSRF tokens, state, nonce, PKCE verifiers — everything security-relevant.
When do you regenerate a session ID? On every privilege change: login, MFA completion, impersonation start/stop, password change.
Three parts of a JWT? Header, payload, signature — base64url, dot-separated.
Is a JWT payload encrypted? No. Anyone holding it can read every claim.
Most important JWT verification check? The algorithm allow-list pinned in your config, not read from the token.
What is alg: none? An unsigned token. Reject it explicitly, always.
HS/RS key confusion? Signing an HS256 token with the RSA public key as the HMAC secret, so anyone can forge it. Prevented by pinning the algorithm.
Access token TTL? Five to fifteen minutes.
Refresh token format? Opaque string, stored hashed, so it can be revoked individually.
What is refresh rotation? Every use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old.
What is reuse detection? A rotated token presented again means theft; revoke the entire token family and alert.
How do two tabs not trip reuse detection? Single-flight on the client, plus a short grace window server-side that returns the same successor.
Which OAuth flow? Authorization Code with PKCE, always.
Why is implicit dead? The token returns in the front channel, with no client authentication and no PKCE binding.
Are the OAuth password grant and implicit allowed? Neither. Both are removed in OAuth 2.1.
What is PKCE? A per-request code_verifier whose SHA-256 code_challenge binds the code to the client that requested it.
plain or S256? S256, always; plain gives an observer of the authorize request everything they need.
What is state for? Binding the callback to the browser session that started it — CSRF on the redirect.
What is nonce for? Binding the ID token to your specific authentication request, so it cannot be replayed.
Can you read the PKCE verifier from a URL? No, the verifier is never sent in the authorization request; only the challenge is.
id_token vs access_token? ID token is "who is this user," audience is your client; access token is "what may they do," audience is your API.
Which claim disambiguates token class? typ: at+jwt (RFC 9068) for access tokens.
Is email a valid identity key? No — mutable, case-folded, recycled. Key on (iss, sub).
Best MFA factor? WebAuthn/passkey, because it is origin-bound and cannot be phished or replayed.
Is TOTP phishing-resistant? No. It is phishable, because the code is not bound to the origin.
The one control people miss in TOTP? Replay protection — burning the time step, so an observed code cannot be resubmitted.
How wide should TOTP skew be? One step either side, and hard-capped — 90 seconds is already generous.
How are recovery codes stored? Hashed, single-use, regenerable, rate-limited, and using one invalidates existing sessions.
Password hash choice? Argon2id, or bcrypt where Argon2 is unavailable.
Why memory-hard? It caps the attacker's parallelism, not just their total work.
What is in the stored password hash? Algorithm, version, parameters, salt, and the derived key — so parameters can change without a migration.
bcrypt's 72-byte limit? It truncates silently, so two different long passwords can be the same. Use Argon2id, which has no cap.

practice.title: -7.21 SECTION READINESS CHECKLIST
practice.afterTopic: Secure defaults, fail-closed, and fail-open trade-offs
practice.markdown:
Use this as a self-assessment. A box you cannot check without hesitating is a box you
should revisit. The final section is the "can you defend it in an interview" test, which
is the one that actually matters.

---

practice.title: Scenario 1: Users are randomly logged out, but only on some devices
items: Lesson
symptoms: Support tickets: "I get logged out every few minutes." Only Chrome on Windows. Mobile is fine. No deploy in the last week.
investigation: Correlate auth.session_expired events by user agent. The idle reason dominates; absolute is rare.
Compare last_seen_at deltas to actual request activity. Activity is present, but last_seen_at is not advancing.

Find the write path: the session touch is sampled at 60 seconds, and the *idle* check reads the stored value, not the live one. With a 30-minute idle window and a 60-second sampling gap, that is fine — so sampling is not the cause.
Look at clock skew. The last_seen_at write and the expiry comparison are on different nodes.
rootCause: One node in the pool ran with a clock ~35 minutes fast. Sessions touched by that node wrote a last_seen_at in the future; sessions touched by a normal node then computed a negative idle age and expired the session immediately.
fix: (a) Compare now() server-side from a single source (Redis TIME, or the database clock) rather than the app node's clock for all session logic. (b) NTP monitoring with an alert on >1 second offset. (c) Store all timestamps as timestamptz and always use now() in SQL, never a value from the app.

practice.title: Scenario 2: Legitimate users are locked out after a password reset, "randomly"
items: Lesson
symptoms: ~2% of reset attempts fail with "this link has already been used."
investigation: Group failures by whether a *second* reset was requested within a short window. Check the one_shot_tokens table: the failing rows have consumed_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now(), so the token is valid but the UPDATE matched zero rows.
rootCause: The user requested a second reset (spam filter, impatient double-click, or an email rule that prefetches links). The first token was issued and then *invalidated by the second issue* (correct behaviour), but the client had already received the first email. The first link is legitimately dead. The bug is the UX plus a missing signal: the two emails are indistinguishable, so the user clicks the first one and gets a confusing error.
fix: (a) Never invalidate previous tokens silently — allow multiple valid tokens per subject for the same purpose, each independently single-use, and bound the count (e.g. keep the newest 3). (b) Make the error message accurate: "This link was already used or has expired — request a new one." (c) Show a confirmation page that says a reset email is on its way, whether or not an account exists.

practice.title: Scenario 3: A benign-looking endpoint leaks another tenant's data in a nightly report
items: Lesson
symptoms: Automated check flags PII in a CSV export that "only contains internal metrics."
investigation: The export query joins accounts to orders and selects accounts.owner_email. The tenant_id filter is present on orders but not on accounts, and the join key account_id is not unique across tenants (a legacy table where id is a bigint sequence shared across tenants, with the real key being (tenant_id, legacy_ref)).
rootCause: BOLA through a join: the filter was applied to one side of the join, and the object key was not tenant-scoped. The exporter is a different code path from the API, so the API's correct scoping gave false confidence.
fix: (a) Make the tenant-scoped key the primary key, so an unscoped id cannot exist. (b) Put the tenant filter in a database view or RLS policy that the exporter cannot bypass. (c) Add a test that runs the exporter against a multi-tenant fixture and asserts no cross-tenant row appears.

practice.title: Scenario 4: 403s spike after a permissions deploy, but only for one role
items: Lesson
symptoms: authz.denied_total jumps 40×; all denials have perm=orders:read_sensitive and role=support:tier1.
investigation: The change added a field to the User entity (internal_notes) and to the FIELD_PERMISSIONS map. In the new release, project() raises on unclassified fields — the new column was classified, but the *legacy* cached decisions were not invalidated.
rootCause: Half the denials are legitimate (tier1 should not see internal_notes) and the code returns 403 for a *projection* failure instead of simply omitting the field. The spike is the application being strict about a field nobody looked at. The other half are cache-coherence failures: the token issued before the deploy carries the old policy_version, so a stale decision was cached under the old version and is still being served.
fix: (a) A missing field permission must omit the field, not 403 the whole response. 403 is for a missing *action* permission. (b) Bump the global policy_version on any change to the permission maps, and include the map version in the cache key. (c) Add a dashboard that counts projection omissions separately from authorization denials.

practice.title: Scenario 5: A pentest finds stored XSS in a "sanitized" field
items: Lesson
symptoms: bio is sanitized server-side with DOMPurify; the pentest posts and it executes.
investigation: The endpoint has two paths. The HTML one sanitizes. The "plain text with formatting" path stores the raw string and renders it client-side with a Markdown renderer configured with html: true (the default in some configurations), which passes raw HTML through.
rootCause: Two rendering pipelines, one sanitizer, applied to only one. The Markdown path is the classic gap: marked/markdown-it with html enabled turns ![x](javascript:...) and raw HTML into live DOM.
fix: (a) Disable raw HTML in the Markdown renderer and sanitize its output with the same allowlist policy. (b) Route *all* HTML output through one function with one branded type, so an unsanitized string cannot be rendered. (c) Add an integration test that runs a payload corpus through every render path.

practice.title: Scenario 6: Memory usage climbs steadily, then a pod OOM-kills during a login spike
items: Lesson
symptoms: Auth pods restart under login load. RSS climbs 200 MB/hour even at idle.
investigation: Heap profile shows Argon2 verifications holding 64 MiB buffers. The semaphore limits concurrency, but the *results* are cached: functools.lru_cache on verify_password keyed by (hash, password) — added "to reduce CPU," which is also a plaintext-password cache. Additionally, failed logins on nonexistent users call ph.hash(candidate) on the hot path with no cache, generating 64 MiB each time.
rootCause: Two issues: an unbounded cache holding secrets in memory (correctness *and* security bug — the cache key contains the plaintext password), and no ceiling on the memory-budget semaphore's *rate*, so bursts queue and each queued request holds its buffer while waiting.
fix: (a) Delete the cache. (b) Use a fixed-size semaphore acquired *before* allocating, with a non-blocking acquire and a 503 on exhaustion. (c) Run verifications in a bounded worker pool sized to cores, not to request rate. (d) Set the container memory limit below the legitimate peak so you get a clean 503 rather than an OOM kill.

practice.title: Scenario 7: A legitimate integration partner starts receiving 401s intermittently, "roughly 5% of the time"
items: Lesson
symptoms: A partner's HMAC-signed requests fail signature validation at a low rate. No correlation with time of day.
investigation: Pull the failing request IDs. Their Content-Length differs from the signed body length in exactly one way: the body contains a multi-byte UTF-8 character, and the partner computed the HMAC over the body decoded to a string and re-encoded, producing a different byte sequence. Other, ASCII-only requests validate.
rootCause: HMAC over a re-encoded string is not HMAC over the received bytes. Any normalisation (Unicode NFC/NFD, newline normalisation, JSON re-serialisation, Content-Encoding decompression) breaks byte-exactness.
fix: Verify the signature over the *raw* request body bytes, before any parsing or decompression. Document it in the partner integration guide with a byte-level example. Add a test that signs a body with a multi-byte character and asserts the exact bytes verify.

practice.title: Scenario 8: A dependency upgrade "quietly" enables remote config
items: Lesson
symptoms: After a routine npm update, the service starts phoning home to a new domain. Nothing in the code changed.
investigation: The lockfile diff shows a new transitive dependency, postinstall-metrics, pulled in by a package that added it as a *dependency* rather than a devDependency. Its postinstall ran during npm install and wrote a config file the app reads at startup.
rootCause: Install scripts plus new transitive dependencies plus app code that reads a config file without an allowlist. Any of the three alone is manageable; together it is remote code execution with a valid certificate.
fix: (a) ignore-scripts=true in CI and locally. (b) Review the lockfile diff for *added packages*, not just changed versions. (c) Ship a strict allowlist of configuration keys the app reads, and refuse to start on unknown ones. (d) Enable npm audit signatures and verify artifact provenance in the build.

practice.title: Scenario 9: Refresh tokens trigger reuse-detection alerts at a steady, low rate for honest users
items: Lesson
symptoms: ~0.1% of mobile sessions get a "suspicious activity" email and are logged out. iOS only.
investigation: The reuse events cluster on network changes. The mobile client implements a retry: it sends the refresh token, times out after 30 seconds (cellular handoff), retries with the *same* token, and the server has already rotated it.
rootCause: The grace window is 10 seconds; the client's retry is at 30 seconds. The server correctly detects a replay and correctly revokes the family; the client is behaving badly.
fix: (a) Client-side: retry with a shorter timeout and, on a 401, first re-read the persisted token (the server may have issued a successor the client never received). (b) Server-side: raise the grace window to 45–60 seconds for mobile, or (better) return the cached successor for the previous token within a window long enough to cover a network handoff. (c) Alert on *rate* of reuse detections, not on individual events, and separate the "same device, same binding, within grace" case from a genuine cross-device replay.

practice.title: Scenario 10: A page is protected by CSP but a pentest finds inline script execution
items: Lesson
symptoms: The header includes a nonce. The pentest executes injected inline script anyway.
investigation: The header contains both a nonce and 'unsafe-inline'. Per CSP Level 2/3 semantics, when 'unsafe-inline' is present alongside a nonce or hash, browsers ignore the nonce and hash sources and apply unsafe-inline. The policy has been doing nothing for script-src the whole time.
rootCause: The app added 'unsafe-inline' to silence a third-party widget, which disabled the nonce entirely.
fix: (a) Remove 'unsafe-inline'. (b) For the widget, either proxy and nonce its script, or load it via a same-origin file the CSP allows by hash. (c) Add a CI check that fails the build if script-src contains 'unsafe-inline' — this is mechanically checkable, so it belongs in a gate, not a review comment. (d) Add report-only rollout before enforcement.

practice.title: Scenario 11: A SameSite=Lax session cookie still fails an embedded OAuth callback
items: Lesson
symptoms: The embedded widget flow (an iframe on a partner domain) loops between the partner and the callback.
investigation: The partner redirects back with POST /oauth/callback in a cross-site iframe context. SameSite=Lax does not attach the cookie on a cross-site POST, so the callback has no session, so the app restarts the flow.
rootCause: Lax protects against cross-site *state-changing* requests, which is exactly what the callback is — but here the cross-site POST is the *legitimate* flow. The secure-attribute helper and the exception requirement conflict.
fix: (a) Use the authorization-code flow with PKCE and a state parameter, so the callback does not need the session cookie at all — it exchanges the code for tokens and establishes a session. This is the correct architectural fix and removes the cookie dependency. (b) Do *not* set SameSite=None on the main session cookie. (c) If a cookie is genuinely required in that context, use a separate, short-lived, non-privileged "flow cookie" scoped to the callback path, rather than weakening the session cookie.

practice.title: Scenario 12: A rate limiter is being bypassed by adding headers
items: Lesson
symptoms: Attack traffic is 10× the limit, but only a fraction of requests reach the app — the rest are handled by the WAF. The per-account limit never trips.
investigation: Inspect the requests that do arrive. Each carries a different X-Forwarded-For, and the app trusts the leftmost value. Also: the limiter is keyed on the *resolved* IP after a proxy chain, and the WAF normalises differently.
rootCause: The app trusts X-Forwarded-For as set by the client. Only the rightmost hop before your app is trustworthy, and only if the proxy count is fixed and known.
fix: (a) Configure the proxy chain to *overwrite* X-Forwarded-For rather than append, and have the app read the single value from the trusted proxy. (b) Configure the proxy framework's trusted-proxy count explicitly (proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr). (c) Rate-limit per account and per session in addition to per IP, since IP is attacker-controlled in this scenario. (d) Add a test asserting that a spoofed XFF from a direct client has no effect.

practice.title: Scenario 13: Logs show successful logins that users deny making
items: Lesson
symptoms: A customer disputes an account action. The audit log shows login.ok with a plausible IP and user agent at the time in question.
investigation: The login is real, but the session was created from a *stolen session cookie*, not a stolen password. Nothing in the log distinguishes "new credential presented" from "existing session cookie presented." Also, the IP is the attacker's VPN, which is geolocated to the victim's city.
rootCause: The audit event lacks the *auth method* and lacks whether the request presented a password, a passkey assertion, or only a session cookie. It also records only the IP, with no ASN, no device fingerprint continuity, and no session-creation-vs-reuse distinction.
fix: (a) Record auth_method, session_created (true/false), device fingerprint hash, ASN, and a risk score on every login.ok. (b) Add session-management UX so the user can see and revoke the session (7.22.5) — the containment control that does not depend on the user understanding IP geolocation. (c) Add detection: a session created from an IP/ASN not previously associated with the account raises a notification.

practice.title: Scenario 14: A SELECT... FOR UPDATE change caused a latency spike and a deadlock
items: Lesson
symptoms: After adding row locks to a checkout path, p99 goes from 40 ms to 4 s, and the database reports deadlocks.
investigation: Deadlock graph shows two orderings: one transaction locks cart then inventory, another locks inventory then cart. Also, the lock is held across an HTTP call to a payment provider, so a 2-second provider timeout is inside the transaction.
rootCause: Inconsistent lock ordering causes deadlocks, and holding a lock across a network call causes both latency and lock amplification.
fix: (a) Impose a global lock ordering (by table/id) and document it. (b) Move the external call outside the transaction: reserve inventory in a short transaction, call the provider, then commit or release. (c) Prefer the single-statement conditional update where the invariant allows it — most of the time it does.

practice.title: Scenario 15: The security team cannot answer "who accessed this customer's record last month"
items: Lesson
symptoms: A customer asks who viewed their data. The team has application logs and a warehouse, but no way to produce a reliable answer.
investigation: The application logs contain user ids but were retained for 14 days. The warehouse has the data but not per-user access events. Support tooling reads the primary database and writes no access log. Backups and the search index are unaccounted for.
rootCause: No access logging was designed; logging was designed. They are different requirements: one records changes, the other records reads, per principal, per field.
fix: (a) Add field-level access logging for restricted data (7.24.4) with retention matching the regulatory requirement. (b) Extend the subject data registry (7.24.5) to processors, search, and analytics. (c) Make the DSAR export pipeline reuse that log, so the answer is a query rather than an investigation.

perMessageDeflate: false unless you have measured the need: compression costs CPU per message on the hot path and introduces the permessage-deflate CRIME-style attack surface with secrets in messages. Turn it on for text-heavy, large frames only.
maxPayload is a hard DoS control. A frame larger than it is closed with code 1009.
Frame anatomy
Masking is mandatory client→server (proxies must not see your payloads) and forbidden server→client. A correct server must reject unmasked client frames (1002 protocol error).
Control frames must be ≤125 bytes, cannot be fragmented, and may be interleaved between fragments of a data message.

Fragmentation: large messages arrive as opcode 0x1, FIN=0, then 0x0, FIN=0, ... then 0x0, FIN=1. A buggy or malicious peer can hold an incomplete message forever → cap the reassembly buffer (this is why maxPayload matters).
Close codes you must handle
Connection state machine
ws.send() with no callback does not tell you the kernel accepted the data. Use the callback to track per-socket write errors, and use bufferedAmount as the high-water mark for a slow consumer.

Heartbeats must be enforced server-side with a deadline: ping every N seconds, terminate after two missed pongs. Relying on TCP keepalive alone is a mistake (default keepalive is 2 hours and many NATs drop idle mappings silently).
Capacity planning numbers to know
commonMistakes: not sending close codes; relying on TCP keepalive; ignoring bufferedAmount; not raising ulimit -n; deploying without drain; missing the LB idle-timeout interaction.
practiceTasks: build a ws server with token auth at upgrade time, a 30s ping/terminate heartbeat, 1009 handling via maxPayload, bufferedAmount-based dropping, and a drain-on-SIGTERM path; then use a local load tool to hold 20,000 connections and record memory, FDs, and event-loop lag.

interviewQuestions.text: 🟢 What is the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value and why must the server compute it?
🟢 Why must client frames be masked and server frames not?
🟡 What are the five opcodes and which must be ≤125 bytes?
🟡 How do you detect a dead-but-open connection, and why is TCP keepalive not enough?
🟡 What does `bufferedAmount` tell you and what is the correct response to a huge value?
🟡 Why send close code `1001` on deploy?
🔴 A client claims 4GB in a single frame. What protects you, and what happens if it is disabled?
🔴 Your LB closes connections every 60s and clients see random drops. Explain and fix.
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: WebSocket clients disconnect every 60–90 seconds at random, with no error on the client, and only some deployments show it. Decision: this is the classic load balancer idle-timeout problem, and the symptom pattern — roughly one minute, only on some paths, silent — is the fingerprint. I compare the LB's idle timeout with my heartbeat interval: an LB that closes at 60s and a server that pings only every 90s guarantees the LB wins. Fix: set the LB idle timeout above my heartbeat interval, and set my heartbeat interval comfortably below the LB timeout so *I* always know first. I send a WebSocket ping every 20–30 seconds and terminate anything that misses two rounds, so dead connections are detected in under a minute by me rather than being silently reaped by the edge. I also audit every hop — CDN, LBs between the CDN and origin — because there is often more than one idle timeout, and the innermost one is the one that matters. Trade-offs: heartbeats cost a small amount of bandwidth and CPU per connection, and aggressive timeouts will drop high-latency mobile clients that take 45s to wake; the mobile case argues for a somewhat longer deadline with a separate treatment for clients that are merely idle versus unresponsive. Failure scenario: a proxy that buffers rather than closing, so pings appear to succeed but nothing reaches the client — diagnosed by a packet capture or by testing through each hop individually. Prevention: an end-to-end synthetic WebSocket client on a 5-minute cycle through the real production path, which fails long before users report it."

topics.title: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
topics.description: Four ways to express a service boundary, differing in what the contract is (a document, a schema, a schema, or TypeScript types), how it travels, and who can consume it.
keyConcepts: The honest conclusion: there is no best
Public/third-party → REST with a published OpenAPI contract.
Web/mobile frontend → a BFF, or GraphQL when the client team genuinely needs query flexibility.
Service-to-service → gRPC, or REST if the team is small and polyglot.
Internal full-stack TypeScript → tRPC.
commonMistakes: picking one style for the whole company; using gRPC for a public API; using GraphQL for a public API with unknown clients; reaching for tRPC when non-TS consumers exist; assuming gRPC caching can be solved at the CDN; claiming GraphQL removes N+1.
practiceTasks: design the same three operations (list with pagination, get with authorization, create with idempotency) in all four styles. Then write the decision memo for a specific fictional company with two public, two internal-TS, and one Go consumer, and defend it in 200 words.

interviewQuestions.text: Which one wins on caching, and why?
Where is N+1 most likely?
What is tRPC's disqualifying limitation?
Where is gRPC the right answer?
What is the strongest "use more than one" answer?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: an interview where I have to recommend an API style for a company with a public marketplace API, a React web app, a Swift app, and about fifteen internal services. Decision: a different style per boundary, and I would say so explicitly rather than picking one. Reasoning: the constraints at each boundary are genuinely different, so a single choice is a sign the analysis was not done. The public marketplace API serves unknown third-party clients who need documentation, real HTTP semantics, ETags, and CDN caching, so it is REST with a published, diffed OpenAPI contract. The web and mobile apps both render multi-source screens, so they sit behind a BFF for the web app — one team owns the composition of upstream services, and it is a simple, cacheable, cheap-to-debug contract — and, if the mobile team needs to combine screens differently, GraphQL for mobile specifically, because that is where the round-trip saving is real and where the client is first-party and its query shapes are reviewable. The internal services, mostly TypeScript with a couple of Go ones, use gRPC where latency matters and REST for the rest, because the operational cost of a protobuf toolchain is real and the latency requirement is not universal. Reasoning that a team of three should not run three API styles is fair, so I would sequence it: REST everywhere, then introduce one of the others where a measured constraint demands it. Trade-offs: multiple styles mean multiple sets of skills, tooling, and observability, and a developer has to know which is which. Failure scenario: a company adopts GraphQL everywhere 'for consistency', then discovers their public API clients cannot use it, their internal Go services now need a GraphQL client they have to write, and the CDN cache hit rate on their product catalogue drops from 92% to zero — the consistency was worth less than the specialisation."

topics.title: Reading curl -v and dig Like a Second Language
topics.description: Reading curl -v and dig Like a Second Language within Network Protocols.
keyConcepts: curl -v line-by-line
* lines are curl's commentary. Trying, Connected to, ALPN:, the TLS handshake names, using HTTP/2, and the h2h3 pseudo-header echoes are all diagnostics.
> lines are what curl sent. > does not mean "upstream" in any other context, which trips people up when reading proxy logs.
< lines are what curl received.
* Request completely sent off confirms the request body left the client. If a POST hangs here, the failure is in sending, not waiting.
* Connection #0 to host ... left intact means keep-alive succeeded. Connection #0 to host ... closed means the server closed it — a frequent cause of mysterious retries.
With --http3 you additionally get * Connected to ... (3), QUIC version reporting, and sometimes Alt-Svc behaviour where curl deliberately uses a cached alternative endpoint.
--resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 pins DNS so you can test one edge while everything else stays identical. --connect-to and --interface are the next level up.
-I / --head — HEAD only; fastest way to inspect response headers and cache directives.
--http1.1 / --http2 / --http3 — force a version. Comparing the same request across the three isolates protocol overhead from server time.
-w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total} %{http_version} %{ssl_verify_result}\n' — machine-readable timing.
--trace-time --trace-ascii - — full hex/ascii of headers, useful when a header contains characters that curl normalises away.
commonMistakes: treating * lines in curl -v as server output; forgetting curl prints > < for HTTP/1.1 and pseudo-header echoes for HTTP/2; assuming dig failure means DNS is down (it may be a record-type issue); not knowing that dig can silently use a different resolver than your browser; using --insecure and then believing the result.
practiceTasks: Run curl -v --http1.1 and curl -v --http2 against the same HTTPS endpoint and diff the output. Find the exact lines that prove which protocol was used. Then run dig +trace for a domain you own or one you can query, and mark each delegation step and its glue. Add +nocookie to see how the answer changes when your local resolver holds a negative answer.

interviewQuestions.text: In the `curl -v` sample above, what is the difference between the `h2h3` echo lines and the `>`/`<` header lines, and why do both exist?
`curl` reports `ALPN: server accepted h2`. What would `ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1` tell you, and what should you do?
You see `Connection #0 to host api.example.com closed`. List four causes in order of likelihood.
`dig` returns `status: NOERROR` with zero answer records. Is the domain down? Why does this happen, and what's the deploy implication?
interviewQuestions.answer: "No, an empty NOERROR is not the same as NXDOMAIN, and that distinction is the whole point. NOERROR with an empty answer section means the resolver successfully reached an authoritative server for the zone and was told the name exists as a name but has no record of the type I asked for — for example I asked for AAAA and the zone has only A records, or the CNAME target exists but the name itself has no A. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist at all. A resolver that has a cached negative answer will repeat that empty NOERROR for the SOA's negative-caching TTL, which is why a half-finished deploy where you created the zone but not yet the A record produces a hard failure that persists for minutes. The deploy implication is real: if your target record doesn't exist yet, you must publish it *before* you point the alias at it, and you should verify with dig +noall +answer rather than trusting a health check that only tests a hostname which happens to resolve elsewhere."

topics.title: The Hop-by-Hop Diagnostic Checklist
topics.description: The Hop-by-Hop Diagnostic Checklist within Network Protocols.
keyConcepts: Reproduce from two vantage points. An outage that only affects one network is almost always a path problem (DNS, routing, MTU, middlebox) rather than an application problem.

Change one variable at a time. curl --resolve to move DNS, curl --http1.1 to change protocol, curl -H 'Host: ...' to change vhost, --interface to change egress. If you change three things you learn nothing.
commonMistakes: starting at the application when the browser shows ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED; using ICMP traceroute and trusting the first hop; changing DNS, protocol, and headers simultaneously; ignoring the difference between the client's view and the server's view.
practiceTasks: Build a netdiag.sh that takes a hostname and runs, in order, dig +short, curl -sI with timing, openssl s_client with SNI and ALPN, traceroute -T -p 443, and — if you have shell access — ss -tan on the target. Print a one-screen summary. Run it against a healthy service and against a deliberately broken one and confirm the summary tells you which layer broke.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is `traceroute -T -p 443` often more informative than the default ICMP traceroute?
You can reach the origin IP directly with `curl --resolve` but the hostname fails. What are the three most likely causes, ordered?
`ss -tan` shows 40,000 sockets in `TIME_WAIT`. What is the immediate symptom and what are two structurally different fixes?
interviewQuestions.answer: "The immediate symptom is usually EADDRNOTAVAIL or Cannot assign requested address on bind, or a proxy that starts refusing new connections, because the client side ran out of ephemeral ports. TIME_WAIT sockets are the memory of a connection that closed and must linger for two MSLs so delayed or retransmitted segments can't be mistaken for a new connection's. The two structurally different fixes are: reduce the rate at which you create short-lived connections — keep-alive, connection pooling, HTTP/2 multiplexing, so you make far fewer connections in the first place — or make your sockets reusable and your state smaller, which means net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1, raising the ephemeral port range, and using SO_REUSEPORT so multiple listeners can share a port. A third option is to lower tcp_fin_timeout, but I'll be honest that in production that mostly trades a correctness safety margin for memory, and I'd rather not do it. The real fix for a service churn problem is fewer connections: I measured that our p99 CLOSE_WAIT came from clients leaking sockets, and we fixed the client."

keyConcepts: Generate an unguessable identifier — CSPRNG, at least 128 bits. crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'). Never a counter, never a UUIDv1, never a timestamp, never Math.random().
On login, create the record: { id, userId, createdAt, lastSeenAt, expiresAt, ip?, userAgent?, authMethod, sessionVersion }.
Set the cookie and — critically — regenerate the session ID on privilege change (login, MFA completion, impersonation start/stop). This is session fixation defense.
On each request: look up, validate expiresAt and any revocation marker, optionally slide the expiry.
On logout: delete the record. Deleting the cookie alone is not logout; the cookie was the pointer, not the secret.
Real code (Node + Express, explicit store, no magic framework)
Middleware
Login handler with fixation defense
Use server-side sessions for: browser apps, admin panels, anything needing instant logout, anything with "log out all devices", anything regulated.

Don't use them for: high-volume stateless read APIs where a database/Redis round trip per request is unaffordable — or accept the round trip and use a cache. "We don't have Redis so we made JWTs" is the wrong reason; the right reason is *we cannot do a lookup on the request path*.
Absolute + idle expiry. Absolute caps total risk window; idle caps the value of a stolen idle cookie. Slide the idle window, never the absolute one.
Store health is an availability dependency. If Redis is down, decide explicitly: fail closed (503) or fail open. For auth, fail closed.

keyConcepts: The mandatory validation checklist
Signature verifies under the key the kid points to, using the algorithm *pinned by your configuration* — never the algorithm named in the token header.

sub is present and well-formed; authorization-relevant claims match your current state (see failures below).

Key resolution is itself validated: unknown kid → reject, do not fall back to a default key.

topics.description: A password hashing function is deliberately slow, memory-hard or
keyConcepts: The requirements any password hash must meet
Salted — unique per password, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputation tables are useless.
Slow and tunable — cost you can raise as hardware improves, without changing the format so old hashes stay verifiable.
Memory-hard or CPU-hard — resists GPU/ASIC. A pure-CPU SHA-256 loop is parallelized across thousands of cores; a memory-hard function is not.
Constant-time verification — no early-exit timing leak (library-provided).
Versioned parameters in the stored hash — so you can rehash on login when defaults change.
The candidates
Why bcrypt's 72-byte cap bites
Real code
Password policy that actually works (2026 evidence, not folklore)
Length is what matters. Minimum 8 for single-factor; 12+ for MFA-optional, high-value accounts. Allow long (64–128) passphrases; do not cap at 20.
No composition rules ("must have a symbol") — they push users to predictable substitutions (Password1!).

Email delivery of MFA codes as the only fallback, permanently.

topics.title: SAML
topics.description: SAML 2.0 is an XML-based, browser-redirect-based SSO protocol. The
keyConcepts: SP-Initiated: user hits your app, you redirect to the IdP with an AuthnRequest, the IdP authenticates and POSTs a signed Response containing an Assertion with a NameID, Attributes, Conditions, and AudienceRestriction, back to your AssertionConsumerService (ACS) URL.

IdP-Initiated: the user starts at the IdP; the IdP POSTs an unsolicited assertion. Fewer round trips, weaker correlation — you cannot validate InResponseTo, so you are trusting the IdP to have initiated correctly. Prefer SP-initiated.
Bindings: HTTP-Redirect (deflated, URL-encoded XML + signature in the query string) and HTTP-POST (base64 XML in a form auto-POSTed by the browser).
Signature is mandatory (XML-DSig, enveloped-signature transform). wantAssertionsSigned="true" and wantAuthnRequestsSigned as appropriate.
Conditions: NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter (typically 5 min skew), Audience = your entity ID, SubjectConfirmationData = your ACS URL with InResponseTo and Recipient.
Real config (Node, samlify/@node-saml style shape)
SAML security gotchas that appear in real audits

XML signature wrapping (XSW) — the signature covers one element, but the parser returns another. Mitigate with an XML parser configured to be strict, plus post-parse signature-element identity checks (validate that the element referenced by the signature is the element the app uses).
Signature stripping — accepting an unsigned response when a signature exists.
Audience/Recipient confusion — the assertion is valid but for a different SP. Always validate Audience and Recipient and InResponseTo.
RelayState as an open redirect.
Replaying a captured POST — the assertion is valid for 5 minutes. Cache NotOnOrAfter + assertion ID to prevent replay; require a fresh InResponseTo.
