topics.title: Security headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options)
topics.description: The controls required because a single endpoint now executes arbitrary selection over a whole graph: per-field authorization, query cost limits, introspection policy, batching limits, and depth limits.
keyConcepts: Query depth and complexity

Depth blocks the recursive pattern (parent { parent { parent ... } }) and cycle exploitation. A max depth of 7-10 for internal apps, 5-6 for public ones. It is cheap, and it catches the obvious abuse.
Complexity is what actually costs you; measure list sizes, not field counts (5.5.3). A static estimator with per-field multipliers plus a per-operation budget is the practical answer.
Timeout: a hard server-side query deadline (AbortSignal or a driver statement timeout) so a query that slipped under the cost budget still cannot run forever.

Also cap: aliases per query, fragment count, introspection depth, the number of variables, and the total request body size. Alias-batching is the most under-appreciated vector — 10,000 aliases of one field is 10,000 units of work in one HTTP request.
Disable introspection in production
Persisted queries / allowlists
Automatic (APQ) — clients may register new queries at runtime. Convenient; still lets an attacker run *any* query your type system allows, subject to depth/complexity limits.

Allowlist — only pre-registered hashes are served. This is genuinely strong: the endpoint becomes a fixed set of operations. It does mean a client with a dynamically-built query needs a registration step, and every client update requires re-registration, so it suits first-party clients and published APIs with managed consumers.
Field-level allowlists per role (a "whitelist graph" of what each role may query) are powerful and brittle; treat them as defence in depth, not the primary control.
Field-level authorization

Defense in depth, in order: database row-level security (or a mandatory tenant predicate in the repository) is the backstop; a directive or a resolver check is the readable layer; a gateway-level field allowlist is the outer layer. Any one of them can be forgotten.
commonMistakes: a per-row authorization query in a field resolver; hoisting one check for the whole list; trusting @skip for access control; believing introspection-off is a security control; no first cap; allowing HTTP batching of operations without per-operation cost limits; interpolating variables into SQL inside a resolver; a GET query in a cookie-authenticated API without CSRF protection.
practiceTasks: add depth and complexity limits, disable introspection, and enable both APQ and allowlist modes (switchable by env) to a GraphQL API. Then attempt, in a test suite: a depth-20 recursive query, a 1,000-alias query, a first: 1000000 query, an orders { canEdit } query on 1,000 rows (count queries before and after batching), an un-registered query under allowlist, a query with a variable from another tenant, and a GET query without a CSRF token.

interviewQuestions.text: Why is a field count a bad complexity measure?
Does `introspection: false` actually secure the API?
What is the N+1 authz trap, and what is the tempting-but-wrong fix?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: a GraphQL API where the team added a canEdit field to Order so the UI could hide an Edit button, and each check was a per-row permissions query. Decision: two changes — batch the check with a DataLoader so it is one query per request, and, more importantly, express the permission as a row filter in SQL rather than a post-filter, so unauthorized orders never leave the database. Reasoning: a per-row authorization check is a database query inside a field resolver, which is the N+1 pattern wearing a security costume. With first: 100 it is 101 queries, and the endpoint is slow for large pages while looking fine in development with five orders. The tempting fix, and the one I have seen in production code reviews, is to hoist the check: fetch the permission once for the current user, then return that single value for every order in the list. That is a data-leak vulnerability, not an optimization — the user is authorized to view *some* orders, so the list is authorized, and now the field reports the same capability for orders they must not touch. The UI would show an Edit button on an order they cannot edit, and any client could act on it. So the rule is: authorization must be evaluated per object, and the cheap way to evaluate it per object is batching, not memoizing. Trade-offs: batching a permission check needs the key to be the object and the value to be a boolean, so you need a well-indexed permissions(order_id, principal_id) table and a query that returns exactly one row per requested id — if the table is missing rows, "absent" must mean "denied", which is an easy thing to get backwards. Failure scenario: a team batches the check correctly, then later optimizes the query with SELECT order_id, bool_or(...) and forgets the tenant_id predicate, so ids from another tenant resolve to false and users see orders they should not see at all — a batching optimization that quietly became a tenant boundary."

topics.title: Secure cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite)
topics.description: Attributes on Set-Cookie that scope the cookie and instruct the browser
keyConcepts: The four that matter, and what each actually buys you
Precise SameSite semantics

Strict — never sent on any cross-site request, including top-level navigations from another site. Breaks inbound links: clicking a Slack link to your app appears logged out. Also does not help a *subresource* request in one specific case: a top-level navigation *from your own site* is same-site even if the link was generated elsewhere.

Lax (the modern browser default) — sent on same-site requests, plus top-level GET navigations that are cross-site. This kills the classic CSRF vectors (auto-submitting forms, GETs, fetch/XHR without credentials) while preserving inbound links. This is the correct default for session cookies.

None — sent everywhere, requires Secure. This is the mode you need for embedded first-party widgets in an iframe, and the mode that removes your CSRF protection. If you use None, you need real CSRF tokens.
Real config (Express)
Host-only vs Domain — pick host-only
Cookie size limits
Do not rely on Path as an access control. A cookie with Path=/admin limits *sending*, not *authority*. Your server must still authorize. Attackers will happily send the header to any path.

Cookie prefixes. __Host- requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain — the browser rejects violations, so it is a free assertion of your intent. __Secure- requires only Secure. Use __Host-sid for your session cookie; you get a hard guarantee against subdomain cookie injection.
Never put two cookies of the same name in one response with different Path/Domain — browsers order unpredictably and you get intermittent auth failures that will consume a week of someone's time.

Cookie jar in SSR. Server-side rendering runs on a shared IP; a server-side cookie jar is a session-fixation vector. Forward the client's Cookie header explicitly and never cache a response containing Set-Cookie across users.

Date: 2026-03-14  Owner: <team>  Status: reviewed

Never use encoding for security. Base64 is not encryption, and an attacker who sees YWRtaW4= already knows the answer. base64 -d is the whole attack.

topics.title: Session cookies: server-side state and why they are still the default choice
topics.description: Server-side sessions: on successful authentication the server mints a
keyConcepts: Generate an unguessable identifier — CSPRNG, at least 128 bits. crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'). Never a counter, never a UUIDv1, never a timestamp, never Math.random().
On login, create the record: { id, userId, createdAt, lastSeenAt, expiresAt, ip?, userAgent?, authMethod, sessionVersion }.
Set the cookie and — critically — regenerate the session ID on privilege change (login, MFA completion, impersonation start/stop). This is session fixation defense.
On each request: look up, validate expiresAt and any revocation marker, optionally slide the expiry.
On logout: delete the record. Deleting the cookie alone is not logout; the cookie was the pointer, not the secret.
Real code (Node + Express, explicit store, no magic framework)
Middleware
Login handler with fixation defense
Use server-side sessions for: browser apps, admin panels, anything needing instant logout, anything with "log out all devices", anything regulated.

Don't use them for: high-volume stateless read APIs where a database/Redis round trip per request is unaffordable — or accept the round trip and use a cache. "We don't have Redis so we made JWTs" is the wrong reason; the right reason is *we cannot do a lookup on the request path*.
Absolute + idle expiry. Absolute caps total risk window; idle caps the value of a stolen idle cookie. Slide the idle window, never the absolute one.
Store health is an availability dependency. If Redis is down, decide explicitly: fail closed (503) or fail open. For auth, fail closed.

topics.title: Cookie security attributes: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain, Path
topics.description: Attributes on Set-Cookie that scope the cookie and instruct the browser
keyConcepts: The four that matter, and what each actually buys you
Precise SameSite semantics

Strict — never sent on any cross-site request, including top-level navigations from another site. Breaks inbound links: clicking a Slack link to your app appears logged out. Also does not help a *subresource* request in one specific case: a top-level navigation *from your own site* is same-site even if the link was generated elsewhere.

Lax (the modern browser default) — sent on same-site requests, plus top-level GET navigations that are cross-site. This kills the classic CSRF vectors (auto-submitting forms, GETs, fetch/XHR without credentials) while preserving inbound links. This is the correct default for session cookies.

None — sent everywhere, requires Secure. This is the mode you need for embedded first-party widgets in an iframe, and the mode that removes your CSRF protection. If you use None, you need real CSRF tokens.
Real config (Express)
Host-only vs Domain — pick host-only
Cookie size limits
Do not rely on Path as an access control. A cookie with Path=/admin limits *sending*, not *authority*. Your server must still authorize. Attackers will happily send the header to any path.

Cookie prefixes. __Host- requires Secure, Path=/, and no Domain — the browser rejects violations, so it is a free assertion of your intent. __Secure- requires only Secure. Use __Host-sid for your session cookie; you get a hard guarantee against subdomain cookie injection.
Never put two cookies of the same name in one response with different Path/Domain — browsers order unpredictably and you get intermittent auth failures that will consume a week of someone's time.

Cookie jar in SSR. Server-side rendering runs on a shared IP; a server-side cookie jar is a session-fixation vector. Forward the client's Cookie header explicitly and never cache a response containing Set-Cookie across users.

topics.title: JWT: structure, verification, and the failure modes everyone hits
topics.description: JSON Web Token: a compact, URL-safe, cryptographically signed set of
keyConcepts: The mandatory validation checklist
Signature verifies under the key the kid points to, using the algorithm *pinned by your configuration* — never the algorithm named in the token header.
alg is in your allow-list. Reject none. Reject HS256 tokens verified with the RS256 public key (key confusion).
Issuer (iss) matches exactly.
Audience (aud) contains your API's identifier — and you reject tokens minted for a different audience (e.g. your frontend's ID token used against your API).
Expiry (exp) is in the future, with clock skew leeway (exp + 60 >= now).
Not before (nbf) has passed, with skew.
iat is plausible and not in the future; exp - iat within your maximum allowed lifetime.
sub is present and well-formed; authorization-relevant claims match your current state (see failures below).
Token type matches the endpoint. An OIDC ID token is not an access token. Rejecting one in the wrong place is a bug class, not a nicety.
Key resolution is itself validated: unknown kid → reject, do not fall back to a default key.
Real code (Node, jose, hardened defaults)

topics.title: Access and refresh tokens, rotation, and revocation
topics.description: A short-lived access token authorizes API calls. A long-lived refresh
keyConcepts: Access token: minutes. Sent on every API request. Verified by the resource server.
Refresh token: hours to days. Sent to the token endpoint only, never to resource servers. Opaque string is strongly preferred — a self-contained refresh token cannot be selectively revoked.
Rotation: every refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one.
Reuse detection: if a refresh token that was already rotated is presented again, assume theft — revoke the entire chain for that grant (RFC 6819 / OAuth 2.0 Security BCP).

Binding: refresh tokens should be bound to the client (public clients to a client-id + a device secret from the OS keystore; confidential clients to their credential) and ideally to a session/grant identifier.
Real code (token endpoint with rotation + reuse detection)
Race conditions in rotation
Revocation
Delete the refresh token record → the access token lives out its remaining TTL.

If instant revocation is required: add jti to a denylist with TTL = exp - now so entries expire naturally. Check the denylist only for privileged routes if you want to preserve the stateless fast path.
Session-level: bump user.sessionVersion.
Authorization-level: on sensitive actions, re-read the user's current permission set — a 10-minute-old token is not evidence of present authority.

Real code (client)

topics.description: OpenID Connect 1.0 is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. It adds the
keyConcepts: id_token vs access_token — the distinction to nail in interviews
Full validation checklist for an id_token (OIDC Core §3.1.3.7)
Issuer (iss) exactly matches the expected issuer identifier (exact string, including scheme, host, path, trailing-slash rules, and case).

topics.title: SAML and enterprise federation awareness
topics.description: SAML 2.0 is an XML-based, browser-redirect-based SSO protocol. The
keyConcepts: SP-Initiated: user hits your app, you redirect to the IdP with an AuthnRequest, the IdP authenticates and POSTs a signed Response containing an Assertion with a NameID, Attributes, Conditions, and AudienceRestriction, back to your AssertionConsumerService (ACS) URL.

IdP-Initiated: the user starts at the IdP; the IdP POSTs an unsolicited assertion. Fewer round trips, weaker correlation — you cannot validate InResponseTo, so you are trusting the IdP to have initiated correctly. Prefer SP-initiated.
Bindings: HTTP-Redirect (deflated, URL-encoded XML + signature in the query string) and HTTP-POST (base64 XML in a form auto-POSTed by the browser).
Signature is mandatory (XML-DSig, enveloped-signature transform). wantAssertionsSigned="true" and wantAuthnRequestsSigned as appropriate.
Conditions: NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter (typically 5 min skew), Audience = your entity ID, SubjectConfirmationData = your ACS URL with InResponseTo and Recipient.
Real config (Node, samlify/@node-saml style shape)
SAML security gotchas that appear in real audits

XML signature wrapping (XSW) — the signature covers one element, but the parser returns another. Mitigate with an XML parser configured to be strict, plus post-parse signature-element identity checks (validate that the element referenced by the signature is the element the app uses).
Signature stripping — accepting an unsigned response when a signature exists.
Audience/Recipient confusion — the assertion is valid but for a different SP. Always validate Audience and Recipient and InResponseTo.
RelayState as an open redirect.
Replaying a captured POST — the assertion is valid for 5 minutes. Cache NotOnOrAfter + assertion ID to prevent replay; require a fresh InResponseTo.

tradeoffs: SAML gives you a mature, widely supported ecosystem and rich attribute

topics.title: Password storage: bcrypt vs argon2 vs scrypt vs PBKDF2
topics.description: A password hashing function is deliberately slow, memory-hard or
keyConcepts: The requirements any password hash must meet
Salted — unique per password, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputation tables are useless.
Slow and tunable — cost you can raise as hardware improves, without changing the format so old hashes stay verifiable.
Memory-hard or CPU-hard — resists GPU/ASIC. A pure-CPU SHA-256 loop is parallelized across thousands of cores; a memory-hard function is not.
Constant-time verification — no early-exit timing leak (library-provided).
Versioned parameters in the stored hash — so you can rehash on login when defaults change.
The candidates
Why bcrypt's 72-byte cap bites
Real code
Password policy that actually works (2026 evidence, not folklore)
Length is what matters. Minimum 8 for single-factor; 12+ for MFA-optional, high-value accounts. Allow long (64–128) passphrases; do not cap at 20.
No composition rules ("must have a symbol") — they push users to predictable substitutions (Password1!).

tradeoffs: Argon2id's memory cost means ~19 MiB per concurrent login; at 1,000 logins/sec you need headroom or you trade memory for latency. bcrypt is CPU-bound and 72-byte capped, which is simpler to reason about but weaker on long passwords. parallelism=1 is right for a web server handling many logins and wrong for a batch job.

topics.title: MFA, TOTP, WebAuthn/passkeys, and recovery codes
topics.description: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from independent
keyConcepts: Factor taxonomy — interview questions test this precision
TOTP (RFC 6238) done correctly
Real code (server-side verification)
The TOTP mistakes that are actually exploitable
No replay protection. Without burning the step, an observer of a shoulder-surfed or phished code can reuse it inside the same 30-second window. This is the most commonly missed control.
Excessive clock skew acceptance. ±5 steps lets a phished code be replayed for minutes.
Rate limiting only by IP. Brute-forcing 6 digits (10^6 codes) is trivial at ~1M attempts; you need a *per-account* rate limit and a lockout/throttle.
Not invalidating the secret on re-enrollment without revoking dependent sessions.
Email delivery of MFA codes as the only fallback, permanently.
TOTP and phishing. TOTP is *phishable*. An attacker proxies the login page and relays the code. Only WebAuthn with origin binding resists this.
Shared secrets stored in plaintext. Encrypt at rest with a KMS key, restrict decrypt to the auth path.
WebAuthn / passkeys done correctly

tradeoffs: Passkeys raise recovery and support costs and have a slower rollout. TOTP

topics.title: SSO patterns, step-up auth, and session lifetime policy
topics.description: SSO is an organizational-level property (one authentication serves many
keyConcepts: Patterns
Step-up authentication mechanics
Session lifetime policy — a table you should be able to recite
Policy mechanics
Idle expiry slides; absolute expiry never slides. A sliding-only policy means a session stolen once is valid forever.
Rotate the session ID on privilege change, and periodically (e.g. every 15 min) to shorten the window for a monitored cookie.
Bind to a coarse device fingerprint for *signals*: if the fingerprint changes unexpectedly, require re-auth instead of terminating (mobile users will thank you).
Do not log out on IP change. Corporate NAT, VPN, mobile handoffs break it constantly; use it as a risk input only.
Global sign-out on password change and on sessionVersion bump.
Use SSO through one IdP; never attempt cross-app SSO via shared cookies in consumer products.
Do not use a parent-domain session cookie unless every subdomain is under the same team, same review process, and same threat model. Prefer an IdP-issued SSO session.
Do not let SSO sessions bypass your own authorization: the IdP authenticates, *you* authorize.

Use static API keys for low-friction third-party integrations, webhook signing secrets, and dev tooling.
Prefer OAuth client credentials (with private_key_jwt or mTLS) for internal services and anything privileged.
Don't use API keys as user authentication. There is no user, no MFA, no session, no revocation granularity.

topics.description: RBAC (role-based) grants permissions to roles and roles to users.
keyConcepts: RBAC mechanics
Role explosion is the classic failure: finance_manager_eu, finance_manager_us, finance_manager_eu_approver. You end up with hundreds of roles and combinatorial assignment.
Seniority inheritance (admin ⊇ all) is convenient and dangerous — it makes the blast radius of a role mistake maximal.
Separation of duties (requester ≠ approver) is a real control that RBAC models awkwardly.
ABAC mechanics
The model that works in practice — hybrid
Real code (single choke point, deny by default)
The scoping layer that prevents IDOR
RBAC for: 5–50 stable capabilities, small teams, admin UIs. Simple to explain, simple to audit, simple to test.
ABAC for: per-record rules, large attribute sets, externalized policy, "finance approver in region X up to $50k."
Do not use a flat permission string per user for anything nontrivial — assignment becomes unmanageable and unreviewable.
Do not use full ABAC from day one for a simple CRUD app. Policy engines are operational machinery; introduce them when the rules genuinely need them.

topics.title: Injection: SQL, NoSQL, command, LDAP
topics.description: Injection occurs when untrusted input is *interpreted* as part of a command,
keyConcepts: SQL injection mechanics
The fix: parameterize everything, and whitelist identifiers

Postgres/psycopg: $1, $2. MySQL: ?. Java/JDBC: ?. .NET: @p. Python: %s with the driver, or ? in the newer API. Node: always ? or $n — never string interpolation, and note that pg's text type plus a JS Array can still produce a mangled IN (...); use pg-format/unnest deliberately.

Dynamic table/column names cannot be parameterized. Use a whitelist map (as above), or a query builder that quotes identifiers — and if you generate SQL identifiers, quote and escape them (", doubled) *and* whitelist.
LIKE injection is a data issue, not a code issue, but still an escape hatch: escape %, _, and the escape character itself, or use a literal-match search.
NoSQL injection
Schema-validate the whole input (e.g. zod) and reject anything that is not a primitive of the expected type. z.string() rejects {$ne: null} before it reaches the driver.
Set mongoose.sanitizeFilter: true, or $eq-wrap every user value: { password: { $eq: req.body.password } }.
Disable server-side JS (security.javascriptEnabled: false) and never pass user input to $where.
Encode user input as a string for operators that expect strings, and use a Document type check.
MongoDB $regex DoS — unanchored regexes over large collections can be an easy DoS. Cap input length and index usage.
Command injection

topics.title: XSS: reflected, stored, and DOM-based, and the encoding rules
topics.description: Cross-site scripting executes attacker-controlled script in another user's
keyConcepts: The three kinds
The real lesson: the output context determines the encoding
The complete, framework-agnostic encoding set (Node)
A real DOM XSS, and its fix
Framework reality, and why frameworks are not enough

React escapes by default; dangerouslySetInnerHTML opts out. Angular sanitizes a known list of contexts but its sanitizer has had bypasses; bypassSecurityTrustHtml is an escape hatch. Vue escapes by default; v-html opts out.

The bypasses are almost always "I need HTML here" (rich text), "I need a URL", or "I need a style". Solve each properly: sanitize rich text with a maintained allow-list sanitizer (DOMPurify on the client, sanitize-html/bleach on the server), validate URLs, and never interpolate into styles.

Server-side rendering changes the calculus. A template engine that escapes is safe; one that does not, or a helper that concatenates HTML, is not. Test the rendered output for <script, onerror=, javascript:, and srcdoc.
Default to text. Ask "do I need HTML at all?" before reaching for a sanitizer. Sanitizers are a second line of defense; a sanitized allow-list is still a large attack surface.
Use textContent for names, emails, comments, and anything a user typed.

Sanitize (never escape) when you genuinely need markup, and sanitize on the server too — the client-side sanitizer protects the current page; the server-side one protects everyone who consumes the data.

CSP as defense in depth does not stop XSS; it stops the *impact* — blocking unsafe-inline means an injected <script> tag will not run, so the attack degrades to attribute-level injection that CSP can also block. It is the highest-value XSS mitigation you can add and it is orthogonal to encoding.

topics.title: CSRF: why SameSite changed the game, and what is left
topics.description: Cross-site request forgery: the victim's browser attaches the victim's
keyConcepts: Why SameSite changed the game
What SameSite=Lax does NOT stop

Top-level cross-site GET navigations still carry the cookie. If any state-changing action is reachable via GET — /logout, /delete?id=1, /transfer?to=..., tracking/pixel endpoints that record an action — it is still CSRF-able.
Anything with SameSite=None — embedded third-party widgets, some enterprise SSO redirects, some legacy integrations.

Subdomain attacks. SameSite is about *site* (registrable domain), not origin. evil.example.com is same-site with app.example.com. If an attacker controls any subdomain, Lax does nothing. This makes __Host- cookies and the absence of Domain= essential.
Older browsers. Support has converged, but if you support them, SameSite is not a control.
Non-cookie ambient credentials — HTTP Basic/Digest auth sent by the browser automatically, and TLS client certificates.
Browser extensions and native clients that ignore the same-origin model.

Login CSRF — forcing a victim to log in as the *attacker's* account, so the victim's data ends up in the attacker's account. SameSite on the session cookie does not prevent this if the login POST itself is a normal same-site flow triggered from a cross-site page that auto-submits to a *different* origin... the session cookie set on that response is what matters, and the attack is about the *victim's* subsequent state.
Defense layers, in order of value
The double-submit cookie pattern
Layer 3: origin/referer checking

topics.title: SSRF: the vulnerability that lives in your server
topics.description: Server-Side Request Forgery: the attacker causes *your* server to make a
keyConcepts: Why it is worse than client-side request forgery
The primitive that makes it work: the redirect
Follow redirects manually and re-validate at every hop
The high-value targets
The defense, layered — and note the ordering matters
Supporting controls (all of them, in production)
Egress firewall / network policy. Deny outbound traffic from the app tier except to a proxy or a known allow-list. This is the control that actually holds when the code has a bug.

Metadata service hardening. AWS: IMDSv2 required (HttpTokens=required). GCP: no automatic GCE_METADATA_HOST exposure on untrusted workloads. Azure: IMDS requires a Metadata: true header (so SSRF alone is not enough) — but a header-injection via an open redirect can still add it.
No ambient cloud credentials in the app. Prefer workload identity with narrow roles over a static key, so a leaked SSRF response is not an account takeover.

Strip or override dangerous request headers on outbound requests: Host, X-Forwarded-*, X-Real-IP, Authorization, Cookie, Proxy-*. An SSRF to your own service with a forged X-Forwarded-For can bypass IP allow-lists.
Do not forward the client's Authorization or cookies to the fetched URL.
DNS pinning to defeat the resolve-then-connect TOCTOU.

keyConcepts: The fix: scope at the data layer, always
Returning 404 vs 403 for out-of-scope objects
The full broken-access-control checklist (from OWASP)
Can a user access another user's data by changing an ID? (IDOR)
Can a user access an admin-only page/API because the client hides the link but the server does not check?
Can a user perform an action out of order — approve without submitting, ship without payment?
Can a user access a resource via an API that lacks the check the web UI has? (The most common real breach: a mobile API or an internal GraphQL endpoint missing a check.)
Can metadata leak: does the API return a user object with more fields than the caller should see, or return 403 vs 200 inconsistently?
Can a user change the tenant or organization in the request body/headers? (Multi-tenancy break)
Are CORS, host header, and X-Forwarded-Host trusted from the client for authorization decisions?
Does the app trust role from a client-side header, JWT claim, or hidden form field?
Can a JWT claim alone grant access without a live authorization check?

Filter the keys in every recursive walk: __proto__, constructor, prototype.

CORS

topics.title: Security headers: CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy
topics.description: HTTP response headers that tell the browser constraints it should enforce
keyConcepts: The full set you should be able to recite, with the reason for each
A production CSP that actually works (nonce-based)
default-src 'none' — deny by default; every capability must be opted in. This is the difference between a policy that survives an addition and one that does not.

script-src with a nonce — the only other way to authorize a script is a hash. 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' must be absent; if script-src contains a nonce or hash, 'unsafe-inline' is ignored by browsers, which is helpful, but do not rely on that.

'strict-dynamic' — a nonce'd script may load further scripts, so you do not have to nonce every dynamically inserted <script>. This is what makes nonces usable in an SPA. It ignores host allow-lists, so do not combine it with a host list (the list is ignored, and a nonce'd script from a compromise can load anything). Pick nonces + strict-dynamic, or a host allow-list, not both.

style-src — nonces for stylesheets work, but inline style *attributes* are not covered by style-src-attr in the same way; if you must allow inline styles, use style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' and accept that risk, or use style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline' only where necessary. Hashes do not work for style attributes.
object-src 'none' — kills plugin content and legacy Flash vectors.
base-uri 'none' — blocks <base href> rewriting, which can hijack all relative URLs (including your script nonces' targets).
form-action 'self' — blocks form exfiltration to an attacker's domain. Frequently forgotten.
frame-ancestors 'none' — replaces X-Frame-Options.
script-src-attr 'none' — blocks inline event handlers (onclick), which is where attribute-based XSS lands.
report-uri / report-to — send violations to your own collector so policy gaps are visible in production. The report body is attacker-influenced: validate size, do not render it, rate-limit it.

tradeoffs: CSP breaks things — that is why report-only exists. strict-dynamic buys

topics.title: Secure file upload
topics.description: File upload is a request to store attacker-influenced bytes on your
keyConcepts: The full threat list for uploads
Real code (the full pipeline)
Storage isolation

Direct-to-object-storage upload (presigned PUT) for large files: it moves the bytes off your servers. You still need the same post-upload verification (type sniff from a ranged read, size, malware scan, promote from quarantine to public) and you must constrain the presigned policy (content-length-range, allowed content types, short expiry, single-use key).
Reject SVG and HTML entirely unless you must support them; if you must, sanitize with a strict allow-list and serve as attachment from the separate origin.
Never "scan by extension."
Do not let uploads be executable: no .php, .jsp, .sh, .html, .svg, .js served from any web-reachable location.
Quarantine → scan → promote is a state machine, and the state must live in the DB with the promotion done by a worker, not by the request handler.
Per-tenant and per-user quotas; alert on a spike in large uploads (a sign of exfiltration).
Log every upload with a hash, so you can answer "was this file served to anyone?" and "is this hash a known-bad sample?"
Retention and deletion: a right-to-delete flow that also deletes the underlying object, including in backups after the retention window.
If you accept documents (PDF, DOCX), consider a separate sandboxed conversion service with a strict resource cap and no network, and treat the original as hostile forever.

tradeoffs: Re-encoding images costs CPU and time but removes EXIF, embedded payloads, and polyglot files — the highest-value single control. Malware scanning adds latency and a dependency; asynchronous scanning with a quarantine state is the usual compromise. Presigned uploads are fast and cheap but move your policy enforcement to a place with less visibility, so the post-upload verification step is not optional.

Never use encoding for security. Base64 is not encryption, and an attacker who sees YWRtaW4= already knows the answer. base64 -d is the whole attack.

Token in the URL → enters Referer headers, browser history, and proxy/CDN logs. Mitigate with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer on the landing page, no third-party assets on it, and short expiry.

Token in the fragment instead of the query — a good pattern: https://app/magic#token=...; the browser never sends the fragment to the server, so the server-side logs never see it; the client posts it. This is what good implementations do.

Prefetch / email-scanner consumption. Corporate link scanners fetch every URL, consuming the single-use token before the user clicks. Mitigate by allowing a *bounded* number of successful consumptions from distinct sources, or by making the first GET not consume — the page then POSTs the token. Or use passkeys instead.
No user enumeration — always 200, same body, comparable timing. Not sending an email to an unknown address leaks existence.
No rate limit — brute force the (32-byte) token is infeasible, but the *email send* must be rate-limited per address and per IP, and the request must be capped to prevent mail-bombing a third party.
No single use — a link that works twice is a persistent credential.

No binding to context — bind to purpose (login vs confirm-email vs reset-password) and, optionally, to the IP/UA that requested it. Never bind a password reset to the session that requested it *only*; also allow it from a different device.
Reused as a password reset. A magic link and a reset link must have different purposes and different records, so a login link cannot reset a password.
No audit trail — magic link issuance and consumption are high-value events for detection.
Passwordless/WebAuthn is the stronger option

# Abuse cases: "bulk invoice upload"

## Assumptions
- The user is authenticated and authorized to upload (permission: invoice:write)
- We assume no account compromise; we defend against the *legitimate* user

## Abuse cases
| # | Abuse | Motivation | Impact | Control | Residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Upload 10M tiny invoices to bloat the table and degrade every query | sabotage / storage cost | High | Per-tenant row-count quota, per-upload row cap (1000), per-tenant insert rate limit, async queue with backpressure | Low |
| A2 | Upload a CSV with 1M columns / a 2GB cell to exhaust parser memory | DoS | High | Byte cap (50 MB), column cap (200), cell cap (32 KB), streaming parse with a row cap, parser in a memory-limited worker | Low |
| A3 | Upload invoices to *another* tenant by putting their tenant_id in the CSV | data poisoning / cross-tenant | Critical | Tenant id comes from the session, never the payload; reject any row whose tenant field differs; log the attempt | None |
| A4 | Repeatedly upload the same file to trigger duplicate-processing bugs (double credit) | fraud | High | Content hash idempotency key unique per tenant; detect and ignore duplicates; alert on high duplicate rate | Low |
| A5 | Use the upload to exfiltrate: reference huge external URLs in cells for the parser to fetch | SSRF via parser | Critical | No network access in the parser; cell content validated against a strict pattern; parser runs sandboxed with egress denied | None |
| A6 | Craft filenames in the CSV to write outside the staging dir (zip slip / traversal) | RCE | Critical | Filenames are ignored; storage keys are generated server-side; extraction validates every entry path | None |
| A7 | Time the bulk job to overlap a reporting window, or hold the queue so others starve | resource capture | Med | Per-tenant concurrency limit, fair scheduling, per-tenant queue depth cap | Low |
| A8 | Upload a file with a formula payload (=cmd|...) then have finance open the export | CSV injection / formula injection | Med | Prefix cells starting with =,+,-,@ with a tab on export; never export user content to Excel unsanitized | Low |
| A9 | Abuse the "undo" to a point beyond the retention window / resurrect deleted invoices | data integrity | Med | Undo is a bounded, logged, permission-checked operation; no resurrection beyond a hard boundary | None |

## Explicitly out of scope
- Credential compromise of another user (handled by auth)
- Physical access
- Denial of service from a distributed botnet (handled by edge rate limiting)

topics.title: Secure defaults, fail-closed, and fail-open trade-offs
topics.description: A *default* is what happens when nobody makes a decision. *Fail-closed*
keyConcepts: Why defaults beat policy
The default-setting surfaces (where defaults actually live)
The fail-closed / fail-open decision, made explicitly per operation
Secure-by-default principles to state in an interview
Deny by default; allow explicitly. A new resource type, route, permission, or IAM rule does not exist until someone creates it with a scope.

The safe action is the one that requires no decision. Default-deny on firewall rules, default-deny IAM, default-required MFA for privileged roles, default no-store on authenticated responses, default redacted logging.
Fail closed for authorization, fail open for data collection. Never trade authorization for availability; do trade a payment's audit event for availability.

Make the insecure path loud and expensive. A feature flag that disables a security control should emit a metric, an audit event, and an alert. Silent degradation is how a temporary decision becomes a permanent hole.

Every default is a decision; record the ones that matter. Where the decision was made, by whom, and when it should be revisited. A default chosen for a 50-person startup is wrong for a regulated enterprise, and nobody will revisit it unless it is written down.

Boring, explicit, and reviewable beats clever. A stack of visible middleware beats a base class that "just handles security" — because the base class is invisible in a code review and its behavior is not discoverable.
Prefer types and typesystems to runtime checks. A repository that cannot be called unscoped, or a TenantId that cannot be confused with a UserId, prevents the bug rather than detecting it.

Verify the defaults are actually in place. Assert them in CI (a test that fails if a route lacks auth, if a security header is missing, if a lockfile is not enforced). A default nobody tests is a default that decays.

keyConcepts: Authentication and credentials
Best password hash today? Argon2id, memory-hard, parameters embedded in the hash.
Why Argon2id over bcrypt? Memory-hardness resists GPU/ASIC; scrypt is the fallback; bcrypt's 72-byte limit is a bug source.
Where does the pepper live? KMS or secret store, never in the database or source control.
How do you stop account enumeration at login? One message, one status, and a dummy verify against a fixed hash for unknown users.
What kills the timing oracle? Performing equivalent KDF work on both paths.
Rehash-on-login: why? Spreads a parameter upgrade across real traffic instead of a batch migration.
Per-account vs per-IP rate limit? Per-account is the one that stops distributed credential stuffing; per-IP is trivially distributed.
Account lockout as a DoS? Yes — an attacker permanently locks a victim. Use a soft challenge before a hard limit, and notify.
MFA factors ranked? Passkey/WebAuthn, then TOTP, then backup codes, then SMS, then email.
Why is SMS weak? SIM swap and SS7 attacks make it the attacker's factor.
Passkey advantage? Phishing-resistant — the credential is bound to the origin.
